{
  "focal_point": "Whether a multiemployer pension plan may retroactively change the actuarial interest-rate assumptions used to calculate an employer’s ERISA/MPPAA withdrawal liability after the liability has been assessed.",
  "legal_provision": "ERISA as amended by the Multiemployer Pension Plan Amendments Act of 1980 (MPPAA), governing withdrawal liability calculations and actuarial assumptions (principally 29 U.S.C. §§ 1381–1405, including § 1393 on actuarial assumptions).",
  "petitioner_position": "Petitioners argue that once a plan assesses withdrawal liability using a set of actuarial assumptions (including the interest rate), the plan cannot later revise those assumptions and apply the revision retroactively to increase the assessed liability. They contend that allowing retroactive assumption changes undermines statutory predictability and fairness in withdrawal-liability assessments, permits funds to “re-price” liability after the fact, and conflicts with the Second Circuit’s decision in Metz, which they characterize as barring retroactive changes to the interest-rate assumption used in the calculation.",
  "respondent_position": "Respondent (supported by the United States, AFL-CIO, and Pension Rights Center) argues that ERISA/MPPAA permits plans to use reasonable actuarial assumptions and to correct or update assumptions consistent with actuarial standards and statutory objectives, including protecting plan solvency and participants’ benefits. They maintain that the statute does not impose the rigid anti-retroactivity rule petitioners propose, and that allowing plans to apply corrected assumptions to the relevant measurement period is consistent with how withdrawal liability is designed to reflect the plan’s unfunded vested benefits rather than lock in an erroneous or outdated rate that would understate liability and shift costs to remaining employers and participants.",
  "key_precedents": [
    "Metz (2d Cir.)",
    "Jacobson v. Fireman’s Fund Ins. Co., 111 F.3d 2d (2d Cir. 1997)"
  ],
  "legal_complexity": "Complex"
}

{
  "focal_point": "Whether New Jersey Transit qualifies as an “arm of the State” entitled to interstate (and related Eleventh Amendment–style) sovereign immunity from private suits in another State’s courts, and how much weight courts must give to the State’s formal financial liability versus other arm-of-the-state factors.",
  "legal_provision": "Interstate sovereign immunity doctrine grounded in the Constitution’s structure (as recognized in Supreme Court precedent) and the Eleventh Amendment framework by analogy; additionally implicated in argument is the New Jersey Tort Claims Act, N.J. Stat. Ann. §§ 59:1-1 to 59:12-3 (as a claimed waiver/limitation on immunity).",
  "petitioner_position": "Galette (and similarly situated respondents in the companion case) argues that NJ Transit should not be treated as an arm of New Jersey for sovereign-immunity purposes because it operates like a public transportation enterprise rather than the State itself, and because arm-of-the-state analysis must consider multiple factors (including how state law characterizes the entity and its operational autonomy) rather than treating the State’s formal exposure to pay judgments as dispositive; Galette also points to New Jersey’s tort-claims framework to argue immunity is limited/waived for certain negligent, ministerial conduct, though the Pennsylvania court viewed that as an improper constructive-waiver theory.",
  "respondent_position": "NJ Transit/New Jersey argues that NJ Transit is an arm of the State and therefore enjoys interstate sovereign immunity, emphasizing that New Jersey bears formal financial responsibility for judgments (or that the State treasury is sufficiently implicated) and that this fiscal-liability factor should carry overriding weight compared to other considerations such as statutory labels or operational features; it also rejects any claimed waiver based on the New Jersey Tort Claims Act absent an unequivocal, express consent to suit in another sovereign’s courts.",
  "key_precedents": [
    "Edelman v. Jordan, 415 U.S. 651 (1974)",
    "Infinity Broad. Corp. v. N.J. Meadowlands Comm’n, 901 A.2d 312 (N.J. 2006)"
  ],
  "legal_complexity": "Complex"
}

{
  "focal_point": "Whether a state prison’s confiscation or destruction of an inmate’s religious property can be challenged for damages under RLUIPA (and/or related federal law), or whether sovereign immunity and the statute’s remedial limits foreclose any meaningful monetary remedy.",
  "legal_provision": "Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA), 42 U.S.C. § 2000cc et seq. (especially § 2000cc-1 and the remedies provision, § 2000cc-2(a)); related sovereign-immunity principles under the Eleventh Amendment and Spending Clause enforcement framework.",
  "petitioner_position": "Landor argues that RLUIPA’s protection for institutionalized persons is undermined if states can substantially burden religious exercise (e.g., by confiscating/destroying religious items) yet avoid any effective remedy; he contends the Fifth Circuit’s approach leaves inmates without compensation even for completed, past harms and invites under-enforcement, and he relies on the statute’s text and purpose—plus the broader Court trend of requiring real remedies for proven religious-liberty violations—to support allowing damages (at least against appropriate defendants) or otherwise rejecting an interpretation that makes RLUIPA largely remediless for past injuries.",
  "respondent_position": "Louisiana argues that even if a burden occurred, RLUIPA does not authorize the monetary relief Landor seeks against the State or state officials in their official capacities because states did not clearly waive sovereign immunity for damages by accepting federal funds; at most, RLUIPA permits prospective injunctive relief, and expanding damages would contradict the statute’s Spending Clause basis, the Court’s sovereign-immunity cases, and the settled understanding that RLUIPA’s remedial scheme is limited.",
  "key_precedents": [
    "Sossamon v. Texas, 563 U.S. 277 (2011)",
    "Tanzin v. Tanvir, 592 U.S. 43 (2020)",
    "Holt v. Hobbs, 574 U.S. 352 (2015)",
    "Cutter v. Wilkinson, 544 U.S. 709 (2005)",
    "City of Boerne v. Flores, 521 U.S. 507 (1997)",
    "Ex parte Young, 209 U.S. 123 (1908)"
  ],
  "legal_complexity": "Complex"
}

{
  "focal_point": "Whether a multiemployer pension plan may retroactively change the actuarial assumptions (especially the interest/discount rate) used to calculate an employer’s ERISA/MPPAA withdrawal liability after the liability has been assessed.",
  "legal_provision": "ERISA as amended by the Multiemployer Pension Plan Amendments Act of 1980 (MPPAA), principally the withdrawal-liability provisions in 29 U.S.C. §§ 1381–1405 (including the calculation rules in § 1393 and related PBGC regulatory framework).",
  "petitioner_position": "Petitioners argue that once a plan assesses withdrawal liability using a set of actuarial assumptions, ERISA/MPPAA does not permit the plan to later revise those assumptions retroactively to increase the assessment. They contend that retroactive assumption changes (notably discount/interest rate changes) undermine statutory finality, predictability, and the employer’s ability to evaluate and arbitrate the assessment, and that at least one circuit precedent (Metz) forbids such retroactive recalculation—making the Fund’s multi-million-dollar increase unlawful.",
  "respondent_position": "Respondents argue that ERISA/MPPAA requires withdrawal liability to reflect the plan’s best estimate of anticipated experience and to be calculated using reasonable actuarial assumptions; if the plan determines that an assumption used in an assessment was incorrect or inconsistent with those requirements, it may correct the calculation even if that entails revising assumptions applied to the assessment. They emphasize protecting plan solvency and participants’ benefits, and they dispute that ERISA creates a categorical bar on post-assessment corrections to assumptions, urging deference to plan actuaries and the statutory scheme’s emphasis on accurate, reasonable valuations.",
  "key_precedents": [
    "Metz (Second Circuit)",
    "Jacobson v. Fireman’s Fund Ins. Co., 111 F.3d 2d (2d Cir. 1997)"
  ],
  "legal_complexity": "Complex"
}

{
  "focal_point": "Whether New Jersey Transit is an “arm of the State” entitled to interstate/Eleventh-Amendment-style sovereign immunity from private suits in another State’s courts, and how much weight courts must give to the State’s formal financial responsibility for judgments in that arm-of-the-state analysis.",
  "legal_provision": "State sovereign immunity doctrine under the U.S. Constitution (including the Eleventh Amendment and the broader interstate sovereign immunity principles recognized by the Supreme Court), as applied through the multi-factor “arm of the State” test; relatedly, New Jersey’s Tort Claims Act (N.J. Stat. Ann. §§ 59:1-1 to 59:12-3) is discussed as a purported waiver but not treated as controlling absent clear consent.",
  "petitioner_position": "Galette (and similarly situated respondents in the companion case) argues that NJ Transit should not be treated as an arm of New Jersey for sovereign-immunity purposes because it operates like a separate, state-created transportation enterprise rather than the State itself; the arm-of-the-state inquiry should be holistic and not dominated by any single factor such as formal state financial liability, and New Jersey’s own statutory/structural characterization of NJ Transit and its operational autonomy should weigh against immunity. Galette also points to New Jersey law (including the Tort Claims Act’s treatment of certain conduct as non-immune) to argue New Jersey has, at least in relevant respects, opened itself (or its entities) to suit—though courts below viewed that as an insufficient/unclear waiver for constitutional sovereign immunity.",
  "respondent_position": "NJ Transit/New Jersey contends NJ Transit is an arm of the State and therefore enjoys sovereign immunity from suits in sister-state courts; the most important indicator is that New Jersey is formally on the hook for judgments (or that judgments implicate the state treasury), and that financial responsibility should carry greater weight than other considerations like labels or operational features. New Jersey also argues that any claimed waiver must be clear and express, and that reliance on state tort-claims provisions or “constructive consent” theories cannot overcome constitutional sovereign immunity.",
  "key_precedents": [
    "Edelman v. Jordan, 415 U.S. 651 (1974)",
    "Infinity Broad. Corp. v. N.J. Meadowlands Comm’n, 901 A.2d 312 (N.J. 2006)"
  ],
  "legal_complexity": "Complex"
}

{
  "focal_point": "Whether an incarcerated person may obtain damages against state prison officials for a substantial burden on religious exercise under RLUIPA, or whether RLUIPA authorizes only prospective injunctive/declatory relief.",
  "legal_provision": "Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA), 42 U.S.C. § 2000cc et seq. (especially § 2000cc-1 and the statute’s “appropriate relief” remedial language), and related sovereign-immunity/Spending Clause enforcement principles.",
  "petitioner_position": "Landor argues that RLUIPA’s authorization of “appropriate relief” for institutionalized persons whose religious exercise is substantially burdened should be read to include damages (at least against officials in their individual capacities), because limiting relief to forward-looking injunctions leaves many completed violations without any meaningful remedy and undermines Congress’s purpose of providing robust protection for prisoners’ religious exercise under a strict-scrutiny standard. Supporting amici contend that damages are consistent with ordinary remedial principles, necessary for deterrence and compensation, and would not create an unmanageable flood of litigation (citing the federal RFRA experience as evidence that strict scrutiny does not overwhelm prison administration).",
  "respondent_position": "Louisiana argues that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize money damages against state officials (particularly in individual capacity) and that, under this Court’s sovereign-immunity and Spending Clause clear-notice doctrines, damages are unavailable absent unmistakably clear statutory language. Respondents maintain that allowing damages would improperly expand state exposure and disrupt prison administration, and that existing avenues—injunctive relief and other legal remedies—are the proper mechanisms for addressing religious-accommodation disputes in prisons.",
  "key_precedents": [
    "Sossamon v. Texas (2011)",
    "Tanzin v. Tanvir (2020)",
    "Cutter v. Wilkinson (2005)",
    "Holt v. Hobbs (2015)",
    "City of Boerne v. Flores (1997)"
  ],
  "legal_complexity": "Complex"
}

{
  "focal_point": "Whether FDA acted arbitrarily and capriciously under the APA when it denied respondents’ premarket tobacco product applications after allegedly directing applicants to follow certain evidentiary standards and then rejecting the applications for not meeting different or heightened requirements.",
  "legal_provision": "Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A) (arbitrary-and-capricious review), in conjunction with the Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act’s premarket tobacco product application (PMTA) regime for “new tobacco products,” 21 U.S.C. § 387j (including the “appropriate for the protection of the public health” standard).",
  "petitioner_position": "FDA argues that its PMTA denials were lawful applications of the Tobacco Control Act’s public-health standard and were not arbitrary or capricious; FDA maintains it could require robust evidence (including evidence bearing on youth initiation and cessation/substitution among adult smokers) and could deny flavored ENDS products when applicants failed to provide sufficient product-specific proof that the benefits to adult smokers outweigh the known risks of youth uptake, notwithstanding general agency guidance or applicants’ claimed reliance interests.",
  "respondent_position": "Respondents argue FDA’s denials were arbitrary and capricious because FDA moved the goalposts—issuing directives and guidance that led applicants to submit certain types of evidence, then denying applications for failing to include other evidence (often characterized as randomized controlled trials or similarly demanding product-specific studies) that FDA had not clearly required; respondents emphasize reliance on FDA’s stated evidentiary expectations and contend the Fifth Circuit correctly set aside the denials as unlawful under the APA.",
  "key_precedents": [],
  "legal_complexity": "Complex"
}

{
  "focal_point": "Whether FDA acted arbitrarily and capriciously under the APA when it denied respondents’ premarket tobacco product applications after applicants allegedly followed FDA’s stated evidentiary directives and standards for ENDS (e-cigarette) products.",
  "legal_provision": "Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A) (arbitrary-and-capricious review), as applied to FDA’s premarket tobacco product application (PMTA) decisions under the Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act (TCA), 21 U.S.C. § 387j (including the “appropriate for the protection of the public health” standard).",
  "petitioner_position": "FDA argues that its PMTA denials were lawful and reasonably explained under the TCA’s public-health standard and the APA, that the agency permissibly required robust evidence (including comparative evidence showing flavored ENDS’ benefits for adult smokers outweigh youth-uptake risks), and that the Fifth Circuit improperly second-guessed FDA’s scientific and policy judgments and mischaracterized FDA’s guidance as binding promises that constrained the agency’s ultimate evidentiary demands.",
  "respondent_position": "Respondents argue FDA’s denials were arbitrary and capricious because FDA shifted or applied evidentiary requirements in a way that contradicted or departed from FDA’s own prior directives and communicated standards for PMTAs (including what types of evidence would suffice), failed to give fair notice or a reasoned explanation for rejecting applications prepared in reliance on FDA’s guidance, and thereby treated similarly situated applicants inconsistently and unlawfully under settled APA principles requiring reasoned decisionmaking and explanation for policy changes.",
  "key_precedents": [],
  "legal_complexity": "Complex"
}

{
  "focal_point": "Whether the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals violated federal law by refusing to grant Richard Glossip a new trial or other relief in a capital case despite the State’s post-conviction concession that serious errors undermined the reliability of his conviction and death sentence.",
  "legal_provision": "U.S. Const. amend. XIV (Due Process Clause) (as applied through doctrines governing fair trial, disclosure of material evidence, and reliability in capital sentencing); and federal constitutional limits on state post-conviction adjudication when a state court rejects a prosecutor/Attorney General confession of error without adequate legal basis.",
  "petitioner_position": "Glossip argues that his conviction and death sentence rest on an unreliable trial infected by material errors tied to the State’s key witness (Justin Sneed) and related evidence, and that Oklahoma’s highest criminal court acted contrary to due process and the heightened reliability required in capital cases by denying relief even after the State’s chief legal officer effectively acknowledged the case could not be defended as fairly tried.",
  "respondent_position": "Oklahoma argues that a state court is not bound by an executive-branch confession of error and must independently determine whether a legally cognizable constitutional violation occurred; on that independent review, the OCCA found no reversible legal error warranting post-conviction relief, and federal review should not convert a prosecutorial concession into an automatic entitlement to vacatur or a new trial.",
  "key_precedents": [
    "Burt v. Titlow, 571 U.S. 12 (2013)",
    "Grzegorczyk v. United States, 142 S. Ct. 2580 (2022) (Kavanaugh, J., statement)",
    "Commonwealth v. Brown, 196 A.3d 130 (Pa. 2018)",
    "Buck v. Davis, 580 U.S. 100 (2017)"
  ],
  "legal_complexity": "Complex"
}

{
  "focal_point": "Whether Title VII permits courts to impose a heightened prima facie burden on “majority-group” plaintiffs—requiring proof of “background circumstances” suggesting the employer is the unusual one that discriminates against the majority—beyond the ordinary McDonnell Douglas framework.",
  "legal_provision": "Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq. (including § 2000e-2’s prohibition on discrimination “because of” race/sex and the associated burden-shifting evidentiary framework used in disparate-treatment cases).",
  "petitioner_position": "Ames argues that Title VII’s text protects “any individual” from discrimination because of protected traits and therefore does not allow courts to demand extra proof from majority-group plaintiffs at the prima facie stage; the Sixth Circuit’s “background circumstances” requirement improperly creates a two-tiered Title VII regime that conflicts with the statute’s equal-treatment principle and the standard McDonnell Douglas prima facie showing.",
  "respondent_position": "The respondent’s position (as reflected in the provided excerpt) emphasizes vehicle/waiver and case-specific posture: Ames did not challenge the Sixth Circuit’s prima facie test in the court below (instead arguing she satisfied it), and in any event the Sixth Circuit affirmed against her on an independent ground—lack of pretext—so even if the Court rejected the “background circumstances” requirement, Ames still could not obtain relief as to the demotion decision; thus the case is a poor vehicle for resolving the broader doctrinal question.",
  "key_precedents": [
    "State v. Sum, 511 P.3d 92 (Wash. 2022) (cited by an amicus as an example of race-conscious standards in state courts)",
    "McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973) (implicit/central to the prima facie and pretext framework discussed in the record)"
  ],
  "legal_complexity": "Moderate"
}

{
  "focal_point": "Whether EPA’s disapproval of individual States’ Good Neighbor SIP submissions for the 2015 ozone NAAQS is a “locally or regionally applicable” action that must be reviewed in the appropriate regional circuit, or a “nationally applicable” action (or one EPA can designate as such) reviewable only in the D.C. Circuit.",
  "legal_provision": "Clean Air Act judicial-review venue provision, 42 U.S.C. § 7607(b)(1) (CAA § 307(b)(1)).",
  "petitioner_position": "Petitioners (States and private parties) argue that SIP disapprovals are quintessentially state-specific actions whose legal effect is limited to the particular State, making them “locally or regionally applicable” under § 7607(b)(1) and therefore reviewable in the relevant regional circuit. They contend EPA cannot convert state-by-state SIP disapprovals into D.C.-Circuit-only cases through labeling or by embedding them in a broader regulatory program, and that allowing such recharacterization would undermine Congress’s cooperative-federalism design by depriving States of regional judicial review for regional decisions.",
  "respondent_position": "Federal respondents (EPA/United States) argue that the challenged SIP disapprovals are properly treated as nationally applicable (or as actions EPA may validly determine have nationwide scope or effect) because they are part of an integrated, multi-state Good Neighbor implementation approach for the 2015 ozone standard, raising uniform, programmatic issues that warrant centralized review in the D.C. Circuit. They also press vehicle/justiciability-type objections to immediate Supreme Court intervention on venue, suggesting the Court should await further merits proceedings, and emphasize that venue can turn on the broader regulatory context rather than the formal state-by-state framing.",
  "key_precedents": [
    "EPA v. EME Homer City Generation, L.P., 572 U.S. 489 (2014)",
    "Mercantile Nat’l Bank v. Langdeau, 371 U.S. 555 (1963)"
  ],
  "legal_complexity": "Complex"
}

{
  "focal_point": "Whether First Step Act § 403’s reduced § 924(c) mandatory consecutive sentencing scheme applies when a defendant was originally sentenced before the Act, that sentence is later vacated, and the defendant is resentenced after the Act’s enactment.",
  "legal_provision": "First Step Act of 2018, § 403 (amending 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) and providing applicability to pre-Act offenses “if a sentence for the offense has not been imposed as of [the] date of enactment”).",
  "petitioner_position": "Petitioners argue that once a pre-Act sentence is judicially vacated, it is treated as a legal nullity and the court must impose a new sentence at resentencing; because that new sentence is imposed after the First Step Act’s enactment, § 403’s anti-stacking reform applies. They contend the Fifth Circuit’s contrary rule elevates a vacated, no-longer-operative sentence over Congress’s instruction to apply the new regime when a sentence “has not been imposed,” undermines the Act’s purpose to eliminate extreme stacked § 924(c) penalties for first-time offenders, and creates arbitrary disparities based on timing and procedural happenstance.",
  "respondent_position": "The United States’ position in the provided materials reflects two phases: (1) in opposition at the certiorari stage, the government argued § 403 does not apply at post-Act resentencings when a sentence had been imposed before enactment, even if later vacated, reading the applicability clause to turn on the historical fact that a sentence once was imposed as of the enactment date; (2) on the merits, the government supports petitioners, agreeing that after vacatur the defendant is resentenced anew and § 403 should apply, emphasizing that vacatur wipes out the prior sentence and that applying § 403 at resentencing better fits the statutory text, ordinary resentencing principles, and Congress’s reform objective to end § 924(c) stacking for first-time offenders.",
  "key_precedents": [],
  "legal_complexity": "Complex"
}

{
  "focal_point": "Whether First Step Act § 403’s reduced mandatory minimums for “stacked” 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) convictions apply when a defendant was originally sentenced before the Act, that sentence is later vacated, and the defendant is resentenced after the Act’s enactment.",
  "legal_provision": "First Step Act of 2018, § 403 (amending 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) and providing that the amendment applies to pre-enactment offenses “if a sentence for the offense has not been imposed as of” Dec. 21, 2018).",
  "petitioner_position": "Petitioners argue that once a pre-Act sentence is judicially vacated, it is treated as a legal nullity, so at the later resentencing the court is imposing a sentence anew; because no valid sentence then exists “as of” the Act’s enactment (or, alternatively, because the relevant sentencing event is the post-Act resentencing), § 403’s anti-stacking reform should apply. They emphasize Congress’s purpose to end the harsh practice of stacking 25-year enhancements on first-time offenders in a single prosecution, and contend that denying § 403 at resentencing irrationally preserves a punishment Congress repudiated, creating arbitrary disparities based on timing and procedural happenstance.",
  "respondent_position": "The United States (in its merits-stage filing supporting Petitioners, notwithstanding its earlier opposition posture) agrees that § 403 applies at a post-Act resentencing after vacatur of a pre-Act sentence. The government’s position is that vacatur wipes out the prior sentence, and at resentencing the court imposes the operative sentence; therefore the defendant falls within § 403’s applicability rule for cases where a sentence had not been imposed in the relevant sense. The government also acknowledges that the Fifth Circuit’s contrary rule improperly denies the benefit of Congress’s reform to defendants whose sentences were set aside and who are being sentenced after the Act.",
  "key_precedents": [],
  "legal_complexity": "Complex"
}

{
  "focal_point": "Whether EPA’s disapproval of individual States’ “Good Neighbor” SIP submissions for the 2015 ozone NAAQS is a “locally or regionally applicable” action that must be reviewed in the regional circuit (here, the Tenth Circuit) rather than exclusively in the D.C. Circuit under the Clean Air Act’s judicial-review venue provision.",
  "legal_provision": "Clean Air Act § 307(b)(1), 42 U.S.C. § 7607(b)(1) (venue for petitions for review of EPA actions; D.C. Circuit for “nationally applicable” actions and regional circuits for “locally or regionally applicable” actions, subject to the statute’s exceptions).",
  "petitioner_position": "Petitioners (Oklahoma, other States, and PacifiCorp) argue that EPA’s challenged actions are state-specific SIP disapprovals whose legal effect is confined to the particular State(s), making them quintessentially “locally or regionally applicable” and therefore reviewable in the appropriate regional circuit. They contend EPA cannot convert state-by-state SIP decisions into “nationally applicable” actions (and thereby force D.C. Circuit venue) through labeling, aggregation, or wordplay, and that the court of appeals erred by treating these SIP disapprovals as nationally applicable for venue purposes.",
  "respondent_position": "Federal respondents (EPA and the United States) argue that the challenged SIP disapprovals are properly treated as nationally applicable (or otherwise within § 7607(b)(1)’s pathway to D.C. Circuit review) because they are part of an integrated nationwide regulatory approach to interstate ozone transport under the Good Neighbor provision and the 2015 ozone NAAQS. On that view, centralized D.C. Circuit review promotes uniformity and avoids fragmented litigation over a coordinated national program, and the Tenth Circuit correctly retained/accepted venue on that basis.",
  "key_precedents": [
    "EPA v. EME Homer City Generation, L.P., 572 U.S. 489 (2014)",
    "Mercantile Nat’l Bank v. Langdeau, 371 U.S. 555 (1963)"
  ],
  "legal_complexity": "Complex"
}

{
  "focal_point": "Whether the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals violated federal constitutional requirements by refusing to grant Richard Glossip a new trial or other relief in a capital case despite the State’s postconviction position and asserted evidence undermining the reliability of the conviction and sentence.",
  "legal_provision": "U.S. Constitution—Fourteenth Amendment Due Process Clause (fair trial; use of false or misleading testimony; suppression of material exculpatory/impeachment evidence under Brady/Giglio/Napue lines) and Eighth Amendment (heightened reliability in capital sentencing).",
  "petitioner_position": "Glossip argues that his conviction and death sentence are constitutionally unreliable because the State’s case depended heavily on cooperating witness Justin Sneed, and postconviction developments (including the Oklahoma Attorney General’s review and asserted concessions) show that material information affecting Sneed’s credibility and the prosecution’s theory was not properly presented to the jury. He contends that due process and the heightened reliability demanded in capital cases require relief (at minimum a new trial), and that the OCCA applied an unduly cramped approach to postconviction review—effectively insulating a potentially wrongful capital conviction even when the State itself acknowledges serious problems.",
  "respondent_position": "Oklahoma maintains that postconviction relief is unavailable absent a legally cognizable constitutional error established under governing standards, and that a prosecutor’s or attorney general’s later change in position (a “confession of error”) does not itself authorize vacatur. The State and supporting amici emphasize that courts must independently assess whether any alleged Brady/Giglio/Napue-type violation or other constitutional defect occurred and whether it was material/prejudicial; they argue the OCCA properly performed that independent review and correctly denied relief under applicable postconviction rules and federal constitutional doctrine.",
  "key_precedents": [
    "Grzegorczyk v. United States, 142 S. Ct. 2580 (2022) (Kavanaugh, J., respecting denial of certiorari) (confession of error does not itself supply a legal basis to vacate)",
    "Commonwealth v. Brown, 196 A.3d 130 (Pa. 2018) (independent judicial review notwithstanding prosecutor’s confession of error)",
    "Buck v. Davis, 580 U.S. 100 (2017) (cited at 580 U.S. 256, 269 in the excerpt) (capital-case reliability and postconviction standards; courts independently assess legal error)"
  ],
  "legal_complexity": "Complex"
}

{
  "focal_point": "Whether an ERISA plaintiff states a prohibited-transaction claim under § 1106(a)(1)(C) by alleging only that the plan paid a service provider (a party in interest) for services, or must also plead that the services were unnecessary or the compensation unreasonable in light of § 1108(b)(2)(A).",
  "legal_provision": "ERISA prohibited-transaction and exemption provisions: 29 U.S.C. § 1106(a)(1)(C) (prohibited transactions with parties in interest) and 29 U.S.C. § 1108(b)(2)(A) (exemption for necessary services at reasonable compensation); related definition of “party in interest,” 29 U.S.C. § 1002(14)(B).",
  "petitioner_position": "Petitioners argue they satisfied every element of § 1106(a)(1)(C) by alleging that plan fiduciaries caused the plans to engage in transactions furnishing services between the plans and service providers who are “parties in interest.” They contend the Second Circuit wrongly required them, at the pleading stage, to negate the § 1108(b)(2)(A) exemption by alleging the services were unnecessary or the fees unreasonable. In their view, § 1108 sets out affirmative defenses/exemptions for defendants to prove, and the circuits are split on this purely legal pleading/burden-allocation issue; the Second Circuit itself acknowledged petitioners would have survived in the Eighth or Ninth Circuits and faced different analyses in other circuits. They also emphasize this case is a clean vehicle because the prohibited-transaction claims were dismissed on a motion to dismiss, squarely presenting what must be pleaded.",
  "respondent_position": "Respondents argue that when the challenged conduct is a routine contract for plan services, the complaint must plausibly allege more than the existence of a service-provider relationship; it must allege facts showing the transaction is actually prohibited—i.e., that the services were not necessary or that compensation was not reasonable—because § 1108(b)(2)(A) expressly removes necessary, reasonably priced service contracts from § 1106’s prohibition. They frame petitioners’ approach as effectively converting ordinary, arm’s-length service arrangements into per se prohibited transactions unless defendants prove an exemption, which (in respondents’ view) is inconsistent with ERISA’s structure and would invite litigation over commonplace plan administration contracts.",
  "key_precedents": [
    "Nachman Corp. v. Pension Benefit Guar. Corp., 446 U.S. 359 (1980)",
    "Dubin v. United States, 143 S. Ct. 1557 (2023)",
    "Braden v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc., 588 F.3d 585 (8th Cir. 2009)",
    "Bugielski v. AT&T Servs., Inc., 76 F.4th 894 (9th Cir. 2023)",
    "Peters (cited at 2 F.4th 199, 244)"
  ],
  "legal_complexity": "Complex"
}

{
  "focal_point": "Whether an ERISA plaintiff states a prohibited-transaction claim under § 1106(a)(1)(C) by alleging that the plan paid a service provider (a party in interest), or must also plead facts negating ERISA’s § 1108(b)(2)(A) exemption (i.e., that the services were unnecessary or the compensation unreasonable).",
  "legal_provision": "ERISA prohibited-transaction and exemption provisions: 29 U.S.C. § 1106(a)(1)(C) (prohibited transactions with parties in interest) and 29 U.S.C. § 1108(b)(2)(A) (exemption for necessary services at reasonable compensation), with “party in interest” defined in 29 U.S.C. § 1002(14)(B).",
  "petitioner_position": "Petitioners argue they pleaded every element of § 1106(a)(1)(C) by alleging that plan fiduciaries caused the plans to furnish services to, and pay compensation to, plan service providers who are “parties in interest.” They contend the Second Circuit wrongly required them at the pleading stage to allege additional facts showing the services were unnecessary or the fees unreasonable—matters that belong to the defendant’s affirmative defense under § 1108(b)(2)(A).
